Spreading and processing gain

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows the rate and integration-time tradeoff that makes a spread waveform recognizable after correlation.

A data bit can multiply a faster known chip sequence. With N = Rc/Rb chips per bit, the matched local code makes the desired chips add coherently over the bit interval. Independent chip noise adds in variance.

In a simple white-noise model whose input bandwidth is approximately the chip rate Rc, processing gain is Gp = Rc/Rb. The dB value is 10 log₁₀Gp. Longer coherent integration is useful only while the local code, carrier phase and data-sign assumptions remain aligned.

Processing gain is a bookkeeping comparison across bandwidth and integration stages. It does not create energy. It also does not suppress every interferer equally; code cross-correlation, spectral placement, receiver saturation and synchronization all matter.

Example

For 100 chips per data bit, the ideal processing gain is 20 dB. An input SNR of −15 dB over the chosen chip-rate noise bandwidth would correspond to about +5 dB at the ideal data decision stage, subject to the model conventions.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. What is the ideal processing gain for 1000 chips per bit?

    Use a power-ratio logarithm.

    10 log₁₀(1000) = 30 dB.

    2. Why can a code-phase mismatch remove much of this benefit?

    The local signs must line up before the sum.

    Wrong local signs cause desired contributions to cancel rather than add coherently. The receiver must acquire and track the code phase and usually carrier Doppler as well.
